list.listitem: The history should focus on training regimen, menstrual history, previous fractures, family history of osteopenia, and signs of disordered eating. C
Explain the potential connection between poor nutrition and caloric intake coupled with increased or intense training and resultant injury and potential adverse health effects. C
Emphasize that overtraining leads to athletes on the sidelines, while individualized and prudent training leads to a healthy, high-performance athlete. C

Management includes optimizing a healthy diet, including adequate calcium and vitamin D intake, restoring regular menstrual cycles, and considering use of behavioral therapy to help athletes manage stress. B

background.definition: The female exercise athlete triad (FEAT), also known as the female athlete triad, was originally defined as amenorrhea, anorexia, and osteoporosis in female athletes. The definition has been broadened to include menstrual dysfunction and disordered eating and how they influence injury and bone mineral density (BMD) in female athletes. Currently, the triad is defined as: (1) low energy availability with or without disordered eating, (2) menstrual dysfunction, and (3) low BMD occurring in physically-active girls and women. This condition is viewed as a spectrum with one end being optimal energy availability, eumenstruation, and optimal bone density and the other as low energy availability, amenorrhea and osteoporosis. Menstrual dysfunction includes amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea, delayed menarche, shortened luteal phase, and anovulation. Disordered eating may present as severe (anorexia or bulimia nervosa) or mild (laxative, diuretic, and diet medication use) disease. The International Olympic Committee in 2014 updated their consensus statement on the Female Athlete Triad further broadening the definition to include the many aspects of impaired physiological function that can occur with an imbalance between dietary energy intake and energy expenditure and to recognize components that occur among male athletes. Impaired physiological function can include disturbed function in metabolic rate, menstruation, bone health, immunity, protein synthesis, and cardiovascular health. The term for this condition is “Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport". Not all conference participants agreed with use of this designation due to insufficient science supporting this change, perceived errors in the presentation of existing literature, and potentially detracting attention away from the well-researched and well-known condition "Female Athlete Triad".

list.listitem: Amenorrhea occurs in 3% to 5% of the general population but has been reported in as many as 15% to 60% of athletic women.
Disordered eating may be as high as 15% to 62% in women college athletes.
The prevalence of anorexia among athletes is similar to that in the general population (1.3%).
The prevalence of bulimia is 8% in athletes and only 4% in the general population.
In a study of high school female athletes, the prevalence of any two of the three triad components was 5.9%; all three components of the triad are present in about 1.2% of female athletes.

In another study of 240 female high school athletes, half reported menstrual irregularity and 42% had 2 or more Triad risk factors (including 143 reporting pressure to be a certain weight, 53 not eating enough, 41 past stress fracture, and 39 past amenorrhea). Knowledge about the Triad was poor among athletes and their coaches.

In one retrospective cohort study of 311 high school athletes, athletes reporting disordered eating (35.4%) were twice as likely to be injured compared to those reporting normal eating behaviors (OR 2.3; 95% CI: 1.4-4.0). Similarly, in a study of 89 female runners competing in interscholastic events, low BMD relative to age (Z-score of ≤−1 SD) and a history of oligo/amenorrhea were significantly associated with an increased occurrence of musculoskeletal injury during the sport season (odds ratio [OR]: 4.6; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.5-13.3; and OR: 4.1; 95% CI: 1.2-13.5, respectively).

With respect to stress fractures, among 259 physically-active girls and women with a mean age of 18.1 ± 0.3 years followed prospectively, 10.8% sustained a bone stress injury or fracture. The incidence of these injuries increased from 5% to 20% for a significant single risk factor to 30% to 50% for significant combined FEAT-related risk factors.

In a study in Japan of 390 female athletes, stress fracture occurred in 9.2% within 3 months. The risk for stress fracture due to the female athlete triad was higher among teens than women in their 20’s with an increased fracture risk of 12.9 times for those with secondary amenorrhea, 4.5 times for those with low BMD, and 1.1 times for those with a low ratio of actual to ideal body weight.

Among 260 elite para athletes in Japan, most (95 male, 65 female) were attempting to change their body composition or weight to improve performance. Bone stress injury was reported in 9.2% and 44% of premenopausal women reported oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea.

Performance variables associated with low energy availability, based on questionnaires completed by 1000 female athletes, included decreased training response, impaired judgement, decreased coordination, decreased concentration, irritability, depression and decreased endurance performance.

Other potential medical complications of the Triad include endocrine, gastrointestinal, renal and neuropsychiatric disorders, and infertility. The 2018 International Olympic Committee statement on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) provide an extensive review of data on these effects for both women and men.
The cause of FEAT is multifactorial and includes inadequate nutrient intake, overtraining, decreased body fat, menstrual irregularity, and emotional stress and pressure.
Low bone density is caused by a lack of sufficient steroid hormones (estrogen and progesterone) and/or a combination of overtraining and insufficient energy replacement through disordered eating.
All three components of FEAT are linked, but it is likely that the combination of menstrual dysfunction and disordered eating gives rise to poor bone mineralization.
Menstrual dysfunction stems from low energy availability that induces exercise-associated hypoestrogenemia and menstrual disturbances.

Some researchers believe that there is a decrease in gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) levels from the hypothalamic/pituitary axis, resulting in less luteinizing hormone (LH) and ultimately menstrual dysfunction. One author posited that reduced LH pulsatility was the change observed resulting from reduced energy availability.
The lack of estrogen and perhaps progesterone decreases the absoption and deposition of calcium into the bone matrix.
Reported biomarkers of low energy availability include decreased triiodothyronine, insulin-like growth factor 1 and leptin, and increased cortisol, ghrelin, and peptide YY.

Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a factor known to regulate bone tissue development and remodeling. In a study of 132 eumenorrheic athletes and 63 athletes with amenorrhea, serum BDNF levels were positively associated with serum estradiol levels and BMD measured at all sites. At 6 months, women prescribed hormone therapy had a significant increase in serum BDNF levels.
In addition, there appears to be a related endothelial dysfunction associated with low serum estrogen and menstrual dysfunction, possibly predisposing these young women to cardiovascular disease.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Lean body sports (distance running, gymnastics, dancing, ice-skating, etc.)

list.listitem: Preparticipation history in athletes should include questions on eating habits and body dissatisfaction. C

The Triad Consensus Panel recommends 11 screening questions including four on menstruation (menses ever, age at onset, most recent and number in last year), four on diet/nutrition (weight concern, attempt to gain/lose weight, food avoidance and eating disorder ever), two on bones (stress fracture or low bone density, ever), and use of female hormones including oral contraceptives (see Questionnaires in Diagnosis, below). C
High drive for thinness was associated with number of in-season injuries in one study of 57 NCAA Division II college female athletes. C

Younger age may also be important in fracture risk; one Japanese study found stress fractures due to the Triad was higher in teenage athletes than for athletes in their 20s. Secondary amenorrhea and low whole-body BMD increased the risk for stress fractures among teenagers by 12.9 times and 4.5 times, respectively. C
History should focus on training regimen, menstrual history, previous fractures, family history of osteopenia, and signs of disordered eating. C
Several risk assessment tools can be helpful for management. C
Physical examination should be performed to identify low body mass index (BMI) and evidence of disordered eating (eg, stained teeth). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Weight loss, heat intolerance, vision changes, exophthalmos, palpitations
Stones (calcium), bones (pain), abdominal groans (nausea, etc.), and psychic moans (altered mentation)
Pallor, fatigue, decreased athletic performance, lightheadedness
Fevers, night sweats, and chills, with unwanted weight loss
Skin pigmentations, weight loss, cold intolerance, fatigue
Unable to participate in routine activities of daily living, blunted affect, depressed mood

list.listitem: History should include any weight loss, questions about body satisfaction or dissatisfaction, decreased caloric intake (consider food diary), and assessment of calcium intake.
Ask about stress fractures, frequent fatigue, amenorrhea, and/or delayed menarche.
Take a careful history of sports participation, training intensity and duration, and previous injuries, especially recurrent or non-healing injuries.

Energy intake is estimated from diet; amounts of 30 kcal/kg of free fat-mass/day or less are associated with detrimental physiologic changes; optimal is 45 kcal/kg free fat mass. Free fat mass can be assessed using weight in kg and body fatness measured through air displacement plethysmography, skin fold measurements, or bioelectrical impedance. A calculator is available to assist with this determination (http://www.femaleathletetriad.org/calculators/).
Energy expenditure can be estimated using the formula metabolic equivalent of task × weight in kilograms × duration of activity in hours.

The 25-item Low Energy Availability in Females (LEAF) Questionnaire had a sensitivity of 78% and specificity of 90% for correctly classifying energy availability, reproductive function, and bone health. Questionnaires to identify eating disorders are also available.

The Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) clinical assessment tool is designed to identify relative energy deficiency, placing athletes into three risk categories based on healthy to disordered eating and its associated metabolic effects (https://bjsm.bmj.com/content/bjsports/49/7/421.full.pdf).

In one study comparing the Triad screening questions to the Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport tool among 166 exercising women, the Triad tool fully cleared fewer women for participation (25.3% vs. 71.7%) and recommended increased surveillance (ie, provisional clearance) of a greater number of athletes (62% vs.18.7%).

Physical examination may show signs of vomiting (eg, dental changes, nail and digit irritation from gagging), cachectic appearance, pallor, tachycardia out of proportion to athlete's fitness, othostatic hypotension, or lanugo.

Low energy availability is indicated by low energy stores such as a BMI <17.5 kg/m2 or in adolescents <85% of expected body weight. If weight is in the normal range, information about food intake and energy expenditure is needed to diagnose low energy availability.
Diagnostic tests should be ordered to rule out secondary causes of amenorrhea and bone loss, as indicated by the clinical history, and to assess severity of these conditions.
Obtain a urine human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) level to exclude pregnancy as a cause of amenorrhea.

In patients with suspected disordered eating, order a basic metabolic profile to assess disordered electrolytes due to poor caloric intake, vomiting, and/or diuretic/laxative use in patients with suspected disordered eating.

Consider obtaining calcium, vitamin D (1,25 OH vitamin D and 25-hydroxy vitamin D), and magnesium levels in patients sustaining frequent or serious stress fracture despite normal diet and intact menstrual function.

The Triad Consensus Panel also recommends obtaining DEXA scans for women with a history of an eating disorder, BMI <17.5 kg/m2 or in adolescents <85% of expected body weight or recent weight loss of >10% in 1 month, menarche at >15 years of age, less than 6 menstrual cycles in a year, and a prior Z-score <−2 after at least one year from baseline DEXA. Other recommendations for DEXA can be found in the panel report referenced here.

An EAT-26 (Eating Attitudes Test) can be given to athletes when an eating disorder is suspected (https://www.seattlechildrens.org/globalassets/documents/healthcare-professionals/pal/eat-26-rating-scale-7.2.pdf).
Begin with an evaluation of menstrual irregularities, diet, bone health, and athletic participation (eg, running logs, hours of ballet/dance per day).
Order laboratory tests for secondary causes of amenorrhea, osteopenia, and disordered eating as indicated, as well as bone density imaging.
Obtain a nutrition evaluation and biopsychosocial evaluation, if needed.

The Triad Consensus Panel recommends a multidisciplinary team for patients with FEAT to include a physician, a sports dietitian, and a mental health professional, if the athlete has disordered eating. Other team members may include an exercise physiologist or certified athletic trainer.

Nonpharmacologic approaches should be used initially; if those efforts fail to restore energy balance with 12 months or there is worsening BMD or fractures, transdermal estrogen with cyclic progesterone should be considered as the next step.
Provide adequate calcium and vitamin D intake through diet or supplements. C
Restore regular menstrual cycle (may take up to one year to restore menses after restoration of energy availability). C
Individualize the training regimen. C
Make behavioral therapy available to help athletes manage stresses of life and sports. C
Use nutritionists and athletic trainers to optimize healthy diet and rehabilitation. C
If using hormone therapy, transdermal estrogen is preferred over oral forms. B

Begin calcium-rich foods or supplements with optimal intake between 1000 and 1300 mg/d and and vitamin D supplementation at 600 IU/day or as needed to maintain a vitamin D level between 32 and 50 ng/mL.

Oral contraceptive therapy has not been consistently associated with improved BMD in amenorrheic athletes and may give the athlete a false perception that energy availability has been restored. This is possibly due to estrogen suppression of IGF-1, a bone trophic factor or method of hormone delivery.

In a recent 3-arm RCT, 121 normal-weight oligo-amenorrhoeic athletes aged 14-25 years were randomized to a 17β-estradiol transdermal patch continuously with cyclic oral micronized progesterone, a combined ethinyl estradiol and desogestrel pill, or no hormone treatment, in addition to calcium and vitamin D supplementation. At 12 months, women randomized to the patch had significantly increased BMD scores at the spine and femoral neck compared to either the pill or control women and increased BMD scores at the hip compared to women on the pill.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 12 RCTs found no differences between traditional cycling of OCs (28-day) and extended (>28 of active hormone) or continuous cycles on contraceptive efficacy and safety profiles. Menstrual symptoms appeared fewer and bleeding patterns were either equivalent or improved with extended or continuous cycles over time. Comparisons on BMD were not reported.

If secondary causes are identified, correct underlying abnormalities (eg, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors [SSRIs] for disordered eating/depression, treatment of hyperthyroidism, or bromocriptine for prolactinoma).
Avoid beginning a bisphosphonate in women of reproductive age due to long-lasting teratogenic effects. There are insufficient data to guide therapy with these agents.

The Triad Consensus Panel did not recommend pharmacologic therapy other than estrogen/progesterone in the absence of a fracture history but other therapies could be considered after failure to respond to non-pharmacologic therapy after 1 year AND low BMD Z-scores with a clinically significant fracture.
Data are also lacking on use of teriparatide or denosomab for osteoporosis treatment in premenopausal women.
Resection of parathyroid adenoma or prolactinoma, if warranted.
The physician should involve a nutritionist, a behavioral therapist, an athletic trainer, the coach, and family members in managing FEAT.
Restore normal menses by correcting nutritional deficits and monitoring overtraining.

Provide nutritional consultation to optimize caloric intake, with a goal of restoring or normalizing body weight and energy balance. Additional targets could be a return to a body weight that restores normal menses this (can occur within several months to a year), a weight gain to achieve a BMI >18.5 kg/m2 or in adolescents >90% of predicted body weight, and a minimum of 2000 kcal/day or more depending on energy expenditure. A goal of restoring menses is particularly important for athletes, and The Triad Consensus Panel recommendations include additional suggestions for achieving these goals.

Behavioral therapy may be effective to help develop positive eating attitudes and nutrition and to avoid overtraining. A Cochrane review identified 10 trials of 599 patients with anorexia nervosa, and concluded that focal psychodynamic therapy was more effective than treatment as usual.
For additional information on eating disorders, see the chapter on anorexia, bulimia and eating disorders.

One study found a positive effect of both athlete-modified dissonance prevention and healthy weight intervention delivered by peers on measures of thin-ideal internalization and dietary restraint at 6 months and bulimic pathology, shape and weight concern at 6 months and one year.
Educate coaches and parents to observe for signs of FEAT, especially among athletes participating in "lean body sports" (eg, track and field, cross-country, gymnastics).
Hospitalize for arrhythmias, electrolyte disturbances, suicidal or homicidal ideation, or unstable fractures (eg, tension sided femoral neck stress fracture).
Refer if moderate or high-risk status (as discussed in follow-up below) to the appropriate member of the multidisciplinary team.
A woman reaches her average peak bone density by age 18 years, with ages 10 to 14 years being the optimal time for bone acquisition. Thus, FEAT can adversely affect bone strength later in life.
Prognosis is good in the context of a multidisciplinary approach is taken and an athletic environment that is supportive, with athletes, coaches, parents, and teammates participating. C
Weekly for initial dietary monitoring if disordered eating is present.

To assist in decisions for clearance for sports participation, the Triad Consensus Panel suggests risk stratification into low, moderate, and high risk groups based on dietary restriction (none, some, eating disorder), BMI (>18.5, 17.6-18.4, <17.5), delayed menarche (<15 years, <16 years, >16 years), oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea in 12 months (>9 menses, 6-9 , <6), BMD (Z-score >−1, <−1 but >−2, <−2), and stress fracture (none, 1, >1 high risk or of trabecular bone sites). One point is given for any moderate risk factor and 2 for any high risk factor. Those with 0 to 1 points may be given full clearance for participation, those with 2 to 5 may be given limited or provisional clearance, and those with >5 points are restricted from training/competition or disqualified.

While potentially useful, this model has not been tested and there is some concern that the return to play recommendations are ambiguous, do not accommodate cumulative risk, and would be difficult to apply in clinical practice.
The Red-S, as noted above, is also a clinical assessment tool that places athletes into three risk categories, but its usefulness as a surveillance tool is unknown.
